draft.title: Text types and forms
card: A form is a kind of text, such as a short story, speech, poem or feature article. Each form has conventions, which are features readers expect to find.
spoken to a live audience. It often speaks to listeners directly, repeats main lines and builds to a call to act or think.
written for print or online. It usually has a headline, an opening that grabs interest, quotes from people and a close look at a topic.
Writers choose a form that suits their purpose and audience, then use its conventions so the text feels right to readers.
draft.remember: Each form has conventions readers expect, so choose the form that fits your purpose and audience.

a.q: What is a convention of a form?
opts: A feature readers expect to find in that kind of text
A rule that stops a writer from changing the text
A fact that a writer must prove with outside evidence
A topic that suits only one kind of text
a.why: Conventions are the features readers expect from a form, such as a headline in a feature article. The option about rules is tempting, but the card says writers use conventions to suit readers, not that they are fixed laws.
a.clue: Think about what readers expect when they pick up a text.

b.q: Jaya wants to persuade her school assembly to start a recycling program. She speaks to the listeners as 'you', repeats a main line and ends with a call to act. Which form is she using?
b.why: Speaking to a live audience, addressing listeners directly, repeating lines and ending with a call to act are speech conventions. A feature article is tempting because it can also persuade, but it is written for readers and has a headline and quotes.
b.clue: Who is listening, and how do they receive the words?

a.best: A feature readers expect to find in that kind of text
